transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I... I came in today because I just, I can’t stop feeling like absolutely everything that goes wrong is my fault. It's just this constant, heavy feeling that follows me everywhere. I work as a business operations specialist, and I've got my bachelor's, so I feel like I should be competent and organized, you know? But lately, every single time there's a tiny mistake at the office, even things I literally cannot control, I just know it's because I'm a terrible employee. I sit there and just ruminate on how I'm ruining the operations. 

And then I go home, and it's the exact same thing there. I bought a house, which I worked really, really hard for, but now I just look around and feel like a completely bad homeowner. If something breaks, or if the yard isn't perfect, or if I just fall behind on regular maintenance, I get this overwhelming sense that I'm negligent and that I actually deserve to lose the house, my job, just... everything I've worked for. It just feels like I'm fundamentally failing at every single aspect of my life and I don't deserve any of the things I have. I just can't get that thought out of my head, no matter what I do or how much I try to reason with myself, it just stays right there, telling me I'm to blame for all of it.
Do you often feel nervous or on edge, aside from these feelings of guilt and inadequacy?

No, not really... I mean, I wouldn't say I feel nervous, exactly. It's not like my heart is racing or I'm waiting for something bad to happen, or like I'm on edge in a panicky way. It's more just... heavy, you know? Like I'm just constantly weighed down by this absolute certainty that I'm messing everything up. I don't get those butterflies in my stomach or that jittery feeling that people talk about when they're anxious. Like, at work, when an invoice gets delayed because a vendor didn't send it on time, I don't feel nervous about my boss finding out. I just feel this crushing, sinking feeling that I should have somehow anticipated it, that I should have emailed them three times instead of two, and that I'm just fundamentally bad at my job. 

And it's the same with the house. I'm not nervously pacing around checking the locks or worrying the roof is going to cave in from a storm. It's just that when I see a water stain on the ceiling, I don't feel anxious, I just feel this deep, dark pit of guilt, like, 'Of course this happened, because I'm a terrible homeowner and I probably neglected something I was supposed to do.' So, no, I don't really feel nervous or on edge, just... just incredibly guilty and exhausted from constantly feeling like I'm doing everything wrong all the time. It's just a totally different feeling than being nervous, if that makes sense.
Do you find yourself enjoying activities or hobbies that you used to like?

Well, no, not anymore. I mean, it’s actually kind of sad when I really stop and think about it, because I used to be such an active person, you know? Like, I used to be the one in my friend group who would always plan our weekend brunches. I’d spend hours looking up new places, checking the menus, making sure there were good options for everyone, and I genuinely loved doing it. It felt good to bring people together. And when I first bought the house, I was so excited to set up the spare room as a painting studio. I bought all these canvases and new brushes, and I’d spend my Sunday afternoons just listening to music and painting. It was so relaxing. 

I was also really big into hiking, especially in the fall when the leaves change. I’d pack a whole lunch and spend the entire day out on the trails. And even with my career, I used to actively seek out networking events. I’d sign up for them, get my business cards ready, and actually look forward to meeting other professionals in operations. I felt driven. But now... now it’s just completely different. All of those things—the brunches, the painting, the hiking, the networking—they don’t bring me any joy at all. If I do manage to drag myself out to see friends or if I sit in front of a canvas, it just feels like this massive chore. It’s like I’m just going through the motions, pretending to care about it because I know I’m *supposed* to like it. But inside, I just feel totally flat and empty. I’d rather just sit on the couch and do absolutely nothing, because even the thought of trying to enjoy something feels exhausting. It’s like the color has just been drained out of everything I used to love.
Do you often feel sad?

Sad? I... I don't know if sad is the right word, honestly. I mean, I don't sit around crying all day, if that's what you mean. It's not like watching a sad movie or, you know, when my childhood dog passed away—that was a very specific, sharp kind of sadness where I was just sobbing and heartbroken. This isn't really like that. It's... it's more like what I was saying before, about feeling heavy and empty. 

I guess you could say I feel down, but it's less about feeling actively sad and more about just feeling completely drained and weighed down by that constant guilt. Like, when I'm sitting on the couch instead of painting, I'm not weeping about not painting. I'm just sitting there, staring at the wall, thinking about how I'm a failure for not doing it, but I don't feel that typical sadness where you need a tissue. I just feel... nothing, really. Or just that heavy, sinking feeling. So, I wouldn't say I feel sad, per se. Just flat. And tired. Really, really tired of feeling like I'm doing everything wrong. Does that make sense? It's just not that crying kind of sad.
How long have you been feeling this way?

Well, let's see... it's been a really long time, honestly. I've been trying to pinpoint exactly when it started, because it didn't just happen overnight, you know? It wasn't like I woke up one Tuesday and suddenly everything was gray and I felt this awful, crushing weight. It was more gradual, like a slow leak in a tire. But if I really think back to when I first started noticing that the things I loved just weren't doing it for me anymore, and when that heavy, flat feeling really set in and wouldn't leave... I'd say it's been about two years and one month. 

I remember because it was right around the time my lease was up on my old apartment, which was a little over two years ago. I was supposed to be packing, and normally I'm so organized—I'm an operations specialist, so logistics are literally my job. I usually have spreadsheets for moving, color-coded boxes, the whole nine yards. But I remember just sitting on the floor of my bedroom, surrounded by empty boxes, and I just couldn't bring myself to care. I didn't want to pack, I didn't care about the new place, I didn't even care if I lost my security deposit. I just sat there feeling completely empty and guilty that I wasn't packing. And it's basically just been a continuation of that exact same feeling ever since. Just this endless stretch of... nothingness and guilt. So yeah, about two years and a month of just feeling completely drained and uninterested in my own life.
Have you noticed a decrease in pleasure from activities you once enjoyed over the past two years?

Well, yes, absolutely. I mean, if I really sit down and look back at the whole timeline of the past two years and a month, that loss of interest—and just that overall low, heavy mood I was telling you about—it’s been there for almost the entire time since this all started. It’s not like it comes and goes, or like I have good months and bad months. It’s just this constant, heavy blanket over everything. 

There were maybe... I don't know, a few very, very brief periods where I could function just a little bit better? Like, I remember there was one week last spring where we had a huge software migration at work. Since I handle operations, I had to coordinate between the IT department and the front-facing staff, making sure the transition didn't disrupt our daily workflow. And for whatever reason, during those few days, I was actually able to get out of bed a bit easier, and I even went to a coffee shop to work for a few hours without feeling completely miserable. I thought, oh, maybe I'm finally snapping out of this, maybe I can go back to painting or maybe I'll actually want to call my friends to get brunch again. 

But then, as soon as the project wrapped up, it was right back to the exact same flat, empty feeling. It’s like those slightly better days were just a tiny glitch, you know? Because other than those incredibly rare, fleeting moments where I could just barely manage to push through and function like a normal person, the lack of pleasure and that dragging low mood have just been... constant. Day in and day out, for the whole two years. It just never really lifts, even when I desperately want it to, which just feeds right back into that guilt I mentioned earlier. I just... I don't understand why those better periods are so short, because it really has just been this one long, unbroken stretch of not enjoying a single thing.
Have you experienced two years or more of persistent feelings of guilt and loss of interest in activities?

Yes, exactly. That's exactly it. The guilt is always there, like I was saying, but the loss of interest is just... it's so stark when I actually sit down and compare it to how I used to be. 

I mean, if you looked at my life two and a half years ago, you honestly wouldn't even recognize me. I used to be the main planner of my friend group. I would plan these big weekend brunches, researching the best spots, making the reservations, coordinating everyone's chaotic schedules—which makes sense, given my job, I'm good at logistics—but I actually loved doing it. It gave me energy. And when I wasn't doing that, I’d be in the spare room of my apartment. I had it completely set up as a little art studio, and I would just paint for hours on end. I'd go hiking on Saturday mornings to get fresh air. I would even go out of my way to sign up for professional networking events! I know a lot of people absolutely dread networking, but I genuinely liked it, just talking business operations and meeting new people in the industry over terrible hotel coffee. 

But now... I don't know, now all of those things just feel like... like tasks. Heavy, impossible tasks that I’m just pretending to care about. If a friend texts about brunch, I just stare at the phone and feel completely exhausted by the idea of having to sit there and fake a smile. The painting supplies in the spare room are just gathering dust, which of course just makes me feel even guiltier because I know I *should* be using them, but I just can't bring myself to pick up a brush. Even the idea of going on a hike or to a networking event makes me feel incredibly tired. It’s all just a performance now, if I do manage to force myself to do any of it. I’m just going through the motions, pretending to care about these things that used to make me who I was. But inside, I just feel completely disconnected from all of it. And it really has been like that this whole time, for those entire two years. Just... pretending.
Do you think your guilt over these things, like being a bad employee or homeowner, is based on realistic assessments of your actions or is it an exaggerated belief that doesn't fit the facts?

Well, see, that's the thing. It's not just a feeling of guilt like, "Oh, I should have painted today." It's... it's much bigger than that, and honestly, it's terrifying. Because even on those very rare days I told you about, those tiny little glitches where I can maybe get out of bed or go to a coffee shop and feel somewhat decent... even then, this other thing doesn't go away. 

It's this absolute certainty that I am being watched. And I don't mean just a vague feeling. I know, I *know* that the mortgage company for my townhouse—because I bought a townhouse a few years ago, right before all this really set in—I know they are monitoring me. Them, and the people at work. The executives, the HR department, probably even the IT guys I was coordinating with during that software migration. I know they are all watching my every move, just waiting for me to slip up. 

They are looking for any tiny mistake, any sign that I'm slipping, so they can finally prove what they already suspect: that I am completely irresponsible, that I'm a fraud, and that I don't deserve any of it. And they're going to use it to take the townhouse away from me. I just know they are building a case. I check my emails constantly, looking for hidden meanings in what my manager says, and every time the mail comes, my heart just pounds because I'm expecting the foreclosure notice or the termination letter. It doesn't matter if I actually completed all my spreadsheets for the week or if my mortgage payment cleared on the first of the month. The facts don't matter because I know what they're planning. So, is it exaggerated? I don't know how it could be, because to me, it is the most real, pressing threat in my life right now. It never stops, doctor. Even when the heavy sadness lifts just a tiny fraction, that fear that they are coming for my home and my job... it's always right there.
Do you think these people, like your manager or the mortgage company, are actually talking about you or planning to take action against you behind your back?

I don't just think it, Doctor, I absolutely know they are. Because... well, because I can actually hear them doing it. It’s not just me reading into an email or overthinking a meeting invite, or just having a bad feeling. I mean, I literally hear them. 

Specifically, there is this one woman... I don't know who she is exactly, if she's someone from HR, or maybe an investigator hired by the mortgage company, but I hear her voice. I'll just be sitting in my townhouse—usually in the living room, right by where the main return vent is for the HVAC system, because the acoustics in these newer builds are so strange anyway and sound really carries—and I will hear her voice coming right through the air vent. Or sometimes it sounds like she's right out in the shared hallway on my floor. And it's not like a muffled whisper where you can't make out the words, it's clear as day. She says things like, “You’re going to lose it all.” Just like that. Over and over. “You're going to lose it all.” 

And it sounds so incredibly real, so physical and present, that I’ve actually stopped whatever I was doing, put my shoes on, unlocked my front door, and gone outside into the hallway to see who was standing out there talking about me. I'll look up and down the corridor, I'll even check the stairwell, trying to catch whoever is spying on me and coordinating this whole thing. But of course, by the time I get out there, the hallway is totally empty. Which just proves they're being incredibly careful, you know? They know I'm onto them. But I hear her. I know she's there, talking about taking my job and my home away from me. So no, it's not just a suspicion I have. I hear it happening with my own two ears.
Do you think the voice you hear through the air vent is real, or could it be a product of your own mind?

I know why you’re asking that. I really do. Because logically, from the outside looking in, I know exactly how it sounds. But you have to understand the difference between a thought and a sound. 

When I’m working on a logistics plan for work, or thinking about my grocery list, that’s in my head. I can feel that it’s inside my brain. But this... this is completely outside of me. Like I was just saying, when I hear that woman’s voice in the hallway, or coming right through the metal grates of the air vent... when she says things like, “You’re going to lose it all”... it has an actual pitch. It has volume. It echoes against the drywall. It’s not an internal monologue, it's a physical sound wave hitting my eardrum. 

It sounds so incredibly, undeniably real that I have literally gone outside into the hallway to see who was there. I wouldn't do that for a thought, you know? I wouldn't stop what I'm doing, physically walk to my front door, unlock the deadbolt, and step out into the corridor just to chase an imagination. I'm a rational person. My entire career in business operations is based on dealing with tangible facts, streamlining processes, and looking at reality. So if it were just my mind playing tricks on me, why would it only sound like it's coming from specific locations, like the vent or the shared wall? Why wouldn't it just follow me around everywhere inside my head? 

So, no, I don't think it's a product of my own mind. I really don't. It's just so frustrating because I know I haven't been able to catch her out there yet, which makes it easy for people to say it's just me, but I know what I'm hearing. I know the difference between my own thoughts and a real person speaking. She's out there. I just... I haven't been fast enough to catch her in the act yet.
Do you experience any sights, smells, or tastes that you think are real but might not be, or is it just the voices you hear?

Well, let me think... sights or smells? No. No, definitely not. I haven't smelled anything strange, like, I don't know, smoke or chemicals or whatever it is people might smell. And I'm not seeing things that aren't there. My vision is perfectly fine. I mean, I stare at complex logistics spreadsheets and data dashboards all day for my job, so I would absolutely notice if my eyes were playing tricks on me or if I was seeing shadows or people in my apartment. So, no, it's nothing like that at all. 

It really is just... it's just the hearing. It's just that voice. And I know I keep coming back to it, but I really need you to understand how incredibly concrete this is for me. It is just that one woman's voice. Like I was explaining, it comes right through the air vent in my living room, or it echoes out in the shared hallway. It’s never a visual thing, it’s just the sound, but it is so, so real. When she says, “You’re going to lose it all,” it’s not some vague impression. It has actual volume. It sounds so completely real that, like I said, I have literally stopped dead in my tracks, put my shoes on, and gone outside into the hallway to see exactly who was out there. 

I check the whole corridor because I know someone is physically speaking those words. If it was just my imagination, I wouldn't be able to hear the way her voice bounces off the drywall, you know? It wouldn't carry through the ductwork of the HVAC system like that. So it's just the voice. No sights, no smells. But honestly, doctor, having someone constantly telling you that you're going to lose it all, hearing that actual voice in your own home... that's more than enough. I don't need to see her to know she's there, waiting for me to fail.
Do you think the woman's voice you hear is something that other people would be able to hear if they were in the room with you?

Yes, absolutely. I mean, without a doubt. Because, like I’ve been trying to explain to you, it is a physical sound. So if someone else was sitting right there on my living room sofa—say, if I had a colleague over to go over some supply chain metrics, or just a friend having coffee—and we were sitting near that main return vent, they would one hundred percent hear her. They would have to! 

Because, again, I know I keep repeating myself with this, but it’s not just a feeling or a thought. When I hear that woman's voice coming through the air vent or out in the hallway, saying, “You’re going to lose it all,” it’s an actual acoustic event. It vibrates the metal grates. It echoes off the walls. If it sounds so incredibly real to me that I’m forced to drop whatever I'm doing, put my shoes on, and physically walk out into the corridor to see who is standing there... well, a guest in my home would hear the exact same thing. It just makes logical sense. My whole job is about analyzing variables and tangible facts, and the fact here is that sound waves don't discriminate, right? If a sound is happening in a room, any functioning human ear is going to pick it up. 

It's actually something I think about a lot, to be honest. I haven't really had anyone over recently because I'm terrified of that exact scenario. I mean, imagine if someone was there and they heard her threatening me through the drywall, telling me I'm going to lose my job and my home? What would I even say to them? How would I explain that HR or the mortgage company has someone outside my door? They’d probably be just as startled as I am. They’d probably want to go out into the hallway to catch her, too, because it's just so loud and clear. So, yes, to answer your question, if someone was in the room, they would absolutely hear her. They couldn't possibly ignore it.
If someone else was in the room with you when you hear the woman's voice, do you think they would hear it too?

I... wait, I feel like I just answered this, didn't I? But, yes. Yes, they absolutely would. I can go over it again if you need me to, because I really need you to understand this part, and maybe I'm not explaining the physics of it clearly enough. 

It’s not just my imagination. I hear this woman’s voice—it’s very distinctly a woman, I can tell by the pitch and the tone of it—and it comes right through the hallway or echoing out of the air vent. And she says things like, "You're going to lose it all." And it sounds so incredibly real, so physically present in the space, that I have gotten up from my spreadsheets, walked to the door, and gone outside to see exactly who was there. I've done it so many times. I wouldn't just drop my work and wander out into a shared corridor for a daydream. 

So if another person was sitting right there next to me, their eardrums would pick up the exact same sound waves. They would hear her saying I'm going to lose it all, just like I do. Because she's actually there, speaking those words into the vent or the hall. So, yes, they would hear it. I'm one hundred percent certain of that, and I don't really know how to make that any clearer.
Have you ever had a period of time where your abnormal thoughts, such as hearing the woman's voice, lasted for less than a month?

Less than a month? No. No, it's... it's been going on for much, much longer than that. It's not something that just pops up for a few weeks and then goes away, I wish it was. It's been a constant, steady thing for... well, let's see. It's been about a year and eight months now. 

I remember exactly when it started, too, because it was right around the end of Q3 the year before last. We were doing our quarterly logistics review, and I was working these incredibly long hours, staring at supply chain metrics until my eyes burned. And that's when I first started noticing the feeling of being watched, you know? Like HR or someone from corporate was monitoring my keystrokes, watching my screen, waiting for me to make a mistake. And then, not long after that, the voice started. At first, it was just a whisper through the vent, but then it got louder, clearer. "You're going to lose it all." 

And it hasn't stopped since. Not for a single month. For a year and eight months, I have been dealing with this woman's voice threatening me, and this constant, heavy feeling that I am being surveilled, that they are just waiting for the moment I slip up so they can take everything away from me. My job, my apartment, everything. It's exhausting, doctor. It's like living in a pressure cooker that never, ever vents. So, no, it's never been just a short-term thing. It's been a year and eight months of this, every single day.
Have you ever seen anything unusual that you couldn't explain, like shadows or figures, in addition to hearing the woman's voice?

No, I haven't seen anything. No shadows, no figures, nothing like that. It's just the voice. I know I've been talking about it a lot, but that's really the only thing. I hear that woman's voice, either out in the hallway or coming through the air vent, and it's always the same sort of thing, telling me, "You're going to lose it all." 

And like I said before, it's not a hallucination where I'm seeing things that aren't there. My vision is perfectly fine. I don't see ghosts or people hiding in the corners. It's purely auditory. But it's so incredibly distinct, so loud and clear, that I really have gotten up from my desk, walked all the way to my front door, unlocked the deadbolt, and stepped out into the corridor just to see who was standing there. Because when you hear someone speaking that clearly, your brain just assumes there's a physical body attached to the voice, right? It just makes sense that someone must be standing right on the other side of the drywall. But when I look, the hallway is completely empty. There's no one there. So, no, I've never seen anything unusual, it's only the voice that I hear.
Do you think there's any possibility that the woman's voice you hear might not be real?

I mean... no. I really don't. And I know we keep circling back to this, and I feel like I'm just repeating myself, but I really need you to understand the logistics of what I'm experiencing here. I just don't see how it could possibly *not* be real. 

When I hear that woman’s voice, whether it's carrying down the hallway or coming right through the metal grating of the air vent, it has actual volume. It has acoustics. It's not just some random thought floating around inside my head. She is physically out there, and she is saying, "You’re going to lose it all." 

And like I was trying to explain earlier, it sounds so incredibly real, so physically present, that I literally stop what I'm doing. Do you know how hard it is to break focus when you're deep in the middle of reconciling operational budgets or mapping out a new workflow? But I drop everything. I push my chair back, I walk to the door, and I go outside into the corridor to see exactly who is standing there. If it wasn't real, why would I do that? Why would I disrupt my own workday to check the hallway or look around the corner by the elevators? 

I know you're asking because you're a doctor and you have to check off certain boxes on your evaluation, but when you hear a voice with your own two ears, vibrating against your own eardrums, you don't just decide it's fake. You just don't. It's real. She's out there. So, no, I don't think there's any possibility that it's just my imagination playing tricks on me.
Do you have any close friends or family members that you talk to regularly?

Well, I do have my sister. We talk... or, I mean, she talks to me, mostly. She calls me, usually on Tuesday evenings after she gets off work, around 6:00 or 6:15, and she'll just talk about her day, her coworkers, her dog... whatever is going on with her. And I listen. I do listen to her. But it's... it's gotten really difficult lately. 

It's hard to explain, but it's like there's this huge disconnect between what I'm hearing and how I'm responding. Like, she'll tell me a story about something funny that happened at the grocery store, or she'll be really upset about something her boss said, and I *know* I'm supposed to react. Logically, my brain registers, "Okay, this is a joke, you should laugh or smile," or "She's upset, you should sound sympathetic." But my face just feels completely blank. It's like the muscles just won't do what they're supposed to do. I just sit there staring at the wall while she's on speakerphone.

And then when it's my turn to talk, when she pauses and waits for me to say something back, it takes so much effort just to form a sentence. I'll just say, "Yeah," or "That's crazy," or "Okay." Just a few words. It feels like my brain is wading through molasses just to get those words out. I used to be able to hold a conversation, you know? Back when I was managing vendor relations, I could talk for hours, negotiate, banter... but now, even with my own sister, it's just exhausting. I know she notices it, too. She'll ask if I'm tired or if I'm not feeling well, and I just don't know how to explain to her that I just... I don't have the energy to make my face move or to string more than three words together. So, yes, I talk to my sister, but it's really not much of a conversation anymore. It's just her talking and me trying to find the energy to pretend I'm still a functioning person.
Do you believe the woman's voice is part of a plot against you?

Well, I wouldn't call it a "plot" exactly, because that makes it sound like some spy movie or something, but... I mean, I know what's happening. I know why she's saying it. It all connects back to the townhouse and my job. 

See, even when I'm having a decent day—like, maybe I actually managed to get out of bed before noon, or I drank a full cup of coffee without feeling like crying—even then, I know they're waiting for me to slip up. The mortgage company, the people at work... they are all watching me. They're watching everything I do. They want me to make a mistake. A big one. Because if I mess up a spreadsheet, or if I miss a deadline on a vendor contract, or if my operational budget is off by even a few cents, they can use that. They can document it, put it in a file, and use it as proof that I'm completely irresponsible. 

And once they prove I'm irresponsible, that's it. That's their leverage to take the townhouse away from me. I bought this place myself, you know? I worked so hard for it. But they want it. I don't know if the mortgage company is talking directly to my supervisors, or if it's just a mutual understanding they have, but they are absolutely coordinating this. They're just waiting for the exact right moment to pull the rug out from under me. 

So when that woman is out in the hallway telling me, "You're going to lose it all," she's not just saying it to be mean. She knows. She knows what they're planning. She's just the one saying it out loud. It's not a hallucination, and it's not a coincidence. It's just a fact. They are watching my every move, waiting for me to fail, so they can take my home. So, yes, the voice is definitely connected to all of that. It's all part of the same thing.
Have you ever had a period where the voice you hear and your feelings of guilt and being watched lasted for less than a month, but then came back?

Less than a month? No... no, I wish it were something that just popped up for a few weeks and then gave me a break. I really do. But it’s not like that at all. It hasn't stopped or paused or faded away for even a single day, let alone a whole month. If I actually sit down and look at the timeline—and I'm very particular about timelines, given what I do for a living—this has been going on for about two years and three months now. It’s just been this one, long, unbroken stretch of time. 

I know exactly when it started, too. It was right after I bought the townhouse. You know, everyone tells you that buying property is this huge milestone, this incredible achievement, especially doing it entirely on your own, on a single income. And I was proud at first. I had all my spreadsheets perfectly organized for the closing costs and the escrow... but almost immediately after I signed the papers and got the keys, this immense pressure just began to build. It was like this suffocating weight settling right on top of my chest. The reality of the thirty-year mortgage, the property taxes, the HOA fees... and knowing that my job is the only thing keeping a roof over my head. 

That pressure just grew and grew, and that's exactly when I started realizing they were watching me, and when that woman started talking to me in the hallway. Two years and three months ago. And it hasn't let up for a second since then, because the mortgage doesn't let up, you know? They never stop watching, so the pressure never stops. I wake up with it, I go to work with it, I sit in my living room with it. So no, it’s never gone away and come back. It's just always there.
Have you ever had a period of time where you heard the woman's voice and believed what she was saying, but then later realized it wasn't real?

Realized it wasn't real? No. No, I mean... why would I think that? It’s not like waking up from a weird dream where you suddenly go, 'Oh, okay, that was just my imagination.' I hear her just as clearly as I’m hearing you right now. 

And, you know, I work in operations. I deal with tangible facts all day long. I deal with metrics, compliance, vendor contracts... I am a very logical, data-driven person. I don’t just invent things out of thin air. When I hear her out there in the hallway, I can hear the actual acoustic echo of the stairwell, you know? I can hear the specific pitch of her voice, the way it bounces off the drywall. And what she’s saying... it aligns perfectly with the actual facts of my situation. Like I was saying before, the mortgage, the people at work waiting for me to make a mistake... if this were just some fake thing my brain was making up, it wouldn't be so perfectly, logically aligned with the literal risks in my life right now. 

So, no, I've never had a moment where I looked back and thought, 'Oh, that wasn't real.' Because it is real. It’s happening. Every single day. Why would I suddenly decide to just... ignore what's right in front of me? It just wouldn't make sense to ignore the data. If I ignored the data at my job, I'd be fired. target_item.manifestation: I hear a woman’s voice in the hallway or through the air vent saying things like, “You’re going to lose it all,” and it sounds so real that I’ve gone outside to see who was there.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether other people would be able to hear the voice, which is a question exploring the nature and my insight regarding my auditory hallucinations.

patient.answer:
I... wait, I feel like I just answered this, didn't I? But, yes. Yes, they absolutely would. I can go over it again if you need me to, because I really need you to understand this part, and maybe I'm not explaining the physics of it clearly enough. 

It’s not just my imagination. I hear this woman’s voice—it’s very distinctly a woman, I can tell by the pitch and the tone of it—and it comes right through the hallway or echoing out of the air vent. And she says things like, "You're going to lose it all." And it sounds so incredibly real, so physically present in the space, that I have gotten up from my spreadsheets, walked to the door, and gone outside to see exactly who was there. I've done it so many times. I wouldn't just drop my work and wander out into a shared corridor for a daydream. 

So if another person was sitting right there next to me, their eardrums would pick up the exact same sound waves. They would hear her saying I'm going to lose it all, just like I do. Because she's actually there, speaking those words into the vent or the hall. So, yes, they would hear it. I'm one hundred percent certain of that, and I don't really know how to make that any clearer.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms meet the criteria for a psychotic episode
doctor.question: Have you ever had a period of time where your abnormal thoughts, such as hearing the woman's voice, lasted for less than a month?

target_item.name: Psychotic Symptoms Duration
target_item.manifestation: The voices and fixed fears about being watched have been present for about a year and eight months.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the duration of my psychotic symptoms (hearing the woman's voice and abnormal thoughts), specifically checking if they lasted for less than a month, which corresponds to the Psychotic Symptoms Duration.

patient.answer:
Less than a month? No. No, it's... it's been going on for much, much longer than that. It's not something that just pops up for a few weeks and then goes away, I wish it was. It's been a constant, steady thing for... well, let's see. It's been about a year and eight months now. 

I remember exactly when it started, too, because it was right around the end of Q3 the year before last. We were doing our quarterly logistics review, and I was working these incredibly long hours, staring at supply chain metrics until my eyes burned. And that's when I first started noticing the feeling of being watched, you know? Like HR or someone from corporate was monitoring my keystrokes, watching my screen, waiting for me to make a mistake. And then, not long after that, the voice started. At first, it was just a whisper through the vent, but then it got louder, clearer. "You're going to lose it all." 

And it hasn't stopped since. Not for a single month. For a year and eight months, I have been dealing with this woman's voice threatening me, and this constant, heavy feeling that I am being surveilled, that they are just waiting for the moment I slip up so they can take everything away from me. My job, my apartment, everything. It's exhausting, doctor. It's like living in a pressure cooker that never, ever vents. So, no, it's never been just a short-term thing. It's been a year and eight months of this, every single day.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's hallucinations are limited to auditory only
doctor.question: Have you ever seen anything unusual that you couldn't explain, like shadows or figures, in addition to hearing the woman's voice?

target_item.name: Hallucinations
target_item.manifestation: I hear a woman’s voice in the hallway or through the air vent saying things like, “You’re going to lose it all,” and it sounds so real that I’ve gone outside to see who was there.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about visual hallucinations (seeing shadows or figures), which falls under the general symptom category of hallucinations.

patient.answer:
No, I haven't seen anything. No shadows, no figures, nothing like that. It's just the voice. I know I've been talking about it a lot, but that's really the only thing. I hear that woman's voice, either out in the hallway or coming through the air vent, and it's always the same sort of thing, telling me, "You're going to lose it all." 

And like I said before, it's not a hallucination where I'm seeing things that aren't there. My vision is perfectly fine. I don't see ghosts or people hiding in the corners. It's purely auditory. But it's so incredibly distinct, so loud and clear, that I really have gotten up from my desk, walked all the way to my front door, unlocked the deadbolt, and stepped out into the corridor just to see who was standing there. Because when you hear someone speaking that clearly, your brain just assumes there's a physical body attached to the voice, right? It just makes sense that someone must be standing right on the other side of the drywall. But when I look, the hallway is completely empty. There's no one there. So, no, I've never seen anything unusual, it's only the voice that I hear.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has any insight into their hallucinations
doctor.question: Do you think there's any possibility that the woman's voice you hear might not be real?

target_item.name: Hallucinations
target_item.manifestation: I hear a woman’s voice in the hallway or through the air vent saying things like, “You’re going to lose it all,” and it sounds so real that I’ve gone outside to see who was there.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the patient's insight into the reality of the voice they hear, which is a direct inquiry into the nature of their hallucinations.

patient.answer:
I mean... no. I really don't. And I know we keep circling back to this, and I feel like I'm just repeating myself, but I really need you to understand the logistics of what I'm experiencing here. I just don't see how it could possibly *not* be real. 

When I hear that woman’s voice, whether it's carrying down the hallway or coming right through the metal grating of the air vent, it has actual volume. It has acoustics. It's not just some random thought floating around inside my head. She is physically out there, and she is saying, "You’re going to lose it all." 

And like I was trying to explain earlier, it sounds so incredibly real, so physically present, that I literally stop what I'm doing. Do you know how hard it is to break focus when you're deep in the middle of reconciling operational budgets or mapping out a new workflow? But I drop everything. I push my chair back, I walk to the door, and I go outside into the corridor to see exactly who is standing there. If it wasn't real, why would I do that? Why would I disrupt my own workday to check the hallway or look around the corner by the elevators? 

I know you're asking because you're a doctor and you have to check off certain boxes on your evaluation, but when you hear a voice with your own two ears, vibrating against your own eardrums, you don't just decide it's fake. You just don't. It's real. She's out there. So, no, I don't think there's any possibility that it's just my imagination playing tricks on me.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has any close relationships
doctor.question: Do you have any close friends or family members that you talk to regularly?

target_item.name: Negative_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: My sister will tell me something funny or upsetting and I know I should react, but my face feels blank and it takes effort to answer with more than a few words.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the patient's social interactions with friends or family, which connects to the patient's negative symptoms involving diminished emotional expression and speech when interacting with her sister.

patient.answer:
Well, I do have my sister. We talk... or, I mean, she talks to me, mostly. She calls me, usually on Tuesday evenings after she gets off work, around 6:00 or 6:15, and she'll just talk about her day, her coworkers, her dog... whatever is going on with her. And I listen. I do listen to her. But it's... it's gotten really difficult lately. 

It's hard to explain, but it's like there's this huge disconnect between what I'm hearing and how I'm responding. Like, she'll tell me a story about something funny that happened at the grocery store, or she'll be really upset about something her boss said, and I *know* I'm supposed to react. Logically, my brain registers, "Okay, this is a joke, you should laugh or smile," or "She's upset, you should sound sympathetic." But my face just feels completely blank. It's like the muscles just won't do what they're supposed to do. I just sit there staring at the wall while she's on speakerphone.

And then when it's my turn to talk, when she pauses and waits for me to say something back, it takes so much effort just to form a sentence. I'll just say, "Yeah," or "That's crazy," or "Okay." Just a few words. It feels like my brain is wading through molasses just to get those words out. I used to be able to hold a conversation, you know? Back when I was managing vendor relations, I could talk for hours, negotiate, banter... but now, even with my own sister, it's just exhausting. I know she notices it, too. She'll ask if I'm tired or if I'm not feeling well, and I just don't know how to explain to her that I just... I don't have the energy to make my face move or to string more than three words together. So, yes, I talk to my sister, but it's really not much of a conversation anymore. It's just her talking and me trying to find the energy to pretend I'm still a functioning person.

inference.note: The patient's symptoms of persistent feelings of guilt, loss of interest in activities, and auditory hallucinations have been present for over two years, which supports the current candidates. The addition of the patient hearing a voice that they believe is real and the presence of delusional thinking about being watched and monitored further supports F22 as a strong candidate.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of delusions of persecution
doctor.question: Do you believe the woman's voice is part of a plot against you?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: Even when I’m having a decent day, I’m still convinced the mortgage company and people at work are watching for mistakes so they can prove I’m irresponsible and take the townhouse from me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I believe the voice is part of a plot against me, which directly relates to my delusions about the mortgage company and coworkers watching me to prove I'm irresponsible.

patient.answer:
Well, I wouldn't call it a "plot" exactly, because that makes it sound like some spy movie or something, but... I mean, I know what's happening. I know why she's saying it. It all connects back to the townhouse and my job. 

See, even when I'm having a decent day—like, maybe I actually managed to get out of bed before noon, or I drank a full cup of coffee without feeling like crying—even then, I know they're waiting for me to slip up. The mortgage company, the people at work... they are all watching me. They're watching everything I do. They want me to make a mistake. A big one. Because if I mess up a spreadsheet, or if I miss a deadline on a vendor contract, or if my operational budget is off by even a few cents, they can use that. They can document it, put it in a file, and use it as proof that I'm completely irresponsible. 

And once they prove I'm irresponsible, that's it. That's their leverage to take the townhouse away from me. I bought this place myself, you know? I worked so hard for it. But they want it. I don't know if the mortgage company is talking directly to my supervisors, or if it's just a mutual understanding they have, but they are absolutely coordinating this. They're just waiting for the exact right moment to pull the rug out from under me. 

So when that woman is out in the hallway telling me, "You're going to lose it all," she's not just saying it to be mean. She knows. She knows what they're planning. She's just the one saying it out loud. It's not a hallucination, and it's not a coincidence. It's just a fact. They are watching my every move, waiting for me to fail, so they can take my home. So, yes, the voice is definitely connected to all of that. It's all part of the same thing.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms meet the criteria for a psychotic episode
doctor.question: Have you ever had a period where the voice you hear and your feelings of guilt and being watched lasted for less than a month, but then came back?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about two years and three months, starting after I bought the townhouse and the pressure of keeping it began to build.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient's symptoms (voices, guilt, delusions) occurred in brief episodes lasting less than a month, which is an inquiry about the overall duration and chronicity of the illness.

patient.answer:
Less than a month? No... no, I wish it were something that just popped up for a few weeks and then gave me a break. I really do. But it’s not like that at all. It hasn't stopped or paused or faded away for even a single day, let alone a whole month. If I actually sit down and look at the timeline—and I'm very particular about timelines, given what I do for a living—this has been going on for about two years and three months now. It’s just been this one, long, unbroken stretch of time. 

I know exactly when it started, too. It was right after I bought the townhouse. You know, everyone tells you that buying property is this huge milestone, this incredible achievement, especially doing it entirely on your own, on a single income. And I was proud at first. I had all my spreadsheets perfectly organized for the closing costs and the escrow... but almost immediately after I signed the papers and got the keys, this immense pressure just began to build. It was like this suffocating weight settling right on top of my chest. The reality of the thirty-year mortgage, the property taxes, the HOA fees... and knowing that my job is the only thing keeping a roof over my head. 

That pressure just grew and grew, and that's exactly when I started realizing they were watching me, and when that woman started talking to me in the hallway. Two years and three months ago. And it hasn't let up for a second since then, because the mortgage doesn't let up, you know? They never stop watching, so the pressure never stops. I wake up with it, I go to work with it, I sit in my living room with it. So no, it’s never gone away and come back. It's just always there.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms meet the criteria for a psychotic episode
doctor.question: Have you ever had a period of time where you heard the woman's voice and believed what she was saying, but then later realized it wasn't real?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the patient's insight into their hallucinations and whether they ever realized the voice wasn't real. The symptom profile does not contain an item specifically addressing insight or a past realization that the symptoms were unreal.

patient.answer:
Realized it wasn't real? No. No, I mean... why would I think that? It’s not like waking up from a weird dream where you suddenly go, 'Oh, okay, that was just my imagination.' I hear her just as clearly as I’m hearing you right now. 

And, you know, I work in operations. I deal with tangible facts all day long. I deal with metrics, compliance, vendor contracts... I am a very logical, data-driven person. I don’t just invent things out of thin air. When I hear her out there in the hallway, I can hear the actual acoustic echo of the stairwell, you know? I can hear the specific pitch of her voice, the way it bounces off the drywall. And what she’s saying... it aligns perfectly with the actual facts of my situation. Like I was saying before, the mortgage, the people at work waiting for me to make a mistake... if this were just some fake thing my brain was making up, it wouldn't be so perfectly, logically aligned with the literal risks in my life right now. 

So, no, I've never had a moment where I looked back and thought, 'Oh, that wasn't real.' Because it is real. It’s happening. Every single day. Why would I suddenly decide to just... ignore what's right in front of me? It just wouldn't make sense to ignore the data. If I ignored the data at my job, I'd be fired. They'd have the excuse they need to let me go. So why would I ignore the data in my own home? I know what I'm hearing, and I know what it means. There's no realization that it's fake because it's just... it's the reality of what I'm dealing with.
